title: Concrete and particularized injury
summary: The claimant must experience an actual or imminent harm to a cognizable interest, including supported economic, aesthetic, recreational, or informational interests.
notes:
An injury in fact is a concrete effect on the claimant, rather than a request to vindicate the general interest in lawful government. Particularization asks how the claimant is affected; concreteness asks whether the asserted harm has sufficient substance. An injury may be widespread and still concrete. Akins allows voters to challenge the denial of useful campaign information, while Sierra Club requires members actually affected by the development of Mineral King.

Environmental plaintiffs must identify their own relationship to the affected place or resource. Lujan rejects indefinite intentions to revisit distant habitats at the summary-judgment stage. Laidlaw accepts evidence that reasonable concerns about ongoing permit violations impaired identified members’ use of a particular river. Those decisions turn on the nature and evidentiary support of the asserted personal injury. They do not make a general interest in environmental protection sufficient.

Congress can recognize legally protected interests, but the assigned TransUnion and Spokeo notes explain a constitutional limit: a statutory violation alone does not automatically create a concrete injury. Tangible harms readily qualify; intangible harms can qualify by a sufficiently close relationship to traditionally recognized injuries. The cases leave contested boundaries between legislative creation of rights and Article III’s independent demands.
